short: Working out what a company or asset is worth, based on the money it should earn, what it owns, or what similar businesses sell for.
kid: Your friend wants to buy your lemonade stand. To pick a fair price, you think about how many coins it will bring in and what other stands have sold for.
detail: Valuation is the process of estimating the economic worth of a business, a share or any other asset. There are three broad approaches. Intrinsic valuation, such as discounted cash flow, values an asset from the cash it is expected to generate and the risk attached to that cash. Relative valuation compares it with similar assets using multiples such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. Asset-based valuation adds up what the assets are worth and subtracts liabilities, which suits holding companies or firms being wound up. Valuation drives IPO pricing, mergers, fundraising and everyday buy or sell decisions; in India, under the rules as of 2025, the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI require a registered valuer's report for certain deals, such as many mergers. The key confusion is between value and price: price is what the market pays today, while a valuation is an estimate built on assumptions, so careful analysts can disagree.
example: Say ABC Ltd is expected to produce steady free cash flow of ₹10 crore a year forever and investors want a 12.5% return. An intrinsic valuation gives ₹10 crore / 0.125 = ₹80 crore. If similar firms sell for 9 times their yearly free cash flow, a relative valuation gives ₹90 crore, showing how methods can differ.

short: What an asset is really worth based on the cash it should produce over its life, which can differ from its market price.
kid: An apple tree that gives you apples every year is worth more than the price someone shouts today. Its real worth comes from all the apples it will give you.
detail: Intrinsic value is an estimate of an asset's fundamental worth, independent of its current market price. For a business it is usually the present value of all the cash it is expected to generate for its owners, discounted at a rate that reflects the risk. Analysts estimate it with discounted cash flow, dividend discount or residual income models. Value investors, in the tradition of Benjamin Graham and Warren Buffett, buy when the price is well below their estimate of intrinsic value and sell when it is well above. It matters because markets can misprice shares for long periods during fear or euphoria. The common confusion is to treat intrinsic value as a precise, knowable number: it is a range that shifts with assumptions about growth, margins and discount rates. In options trading the same phrase has a separate meaning: the amount by which an option is in the money.
example: Say XYZ Ltd is expected to pay its owners ₹20 per share every year forever, and investors require 10% a year. Its intrinsic value is ₹20 / 0.10 = ₹200 per share. If the share trades at ₹150, it looks undervalued by ₹50, or 25% of intrinsic value.
formula: Intrinsic value = sum of CFt / (1 + r)^t over the asset's life, where CFt is the expected cash flow in year t and r is the required return

short: The gap between what you think an investment is worth and the lower price you pay, kept as a cushion against mistakes.
kid: If a bridge only needs to hold 10 trucks, builders make it strong enough for 20. Paying much less than something is worth works the same way, so a small mistake does not hurt you.
detail: Margin of safety, a principle popularised by Benjamin Graham in The Intelligent Investor, means buying an asset only when its price is well below your estimate of its intrinsic value. Because every valuation rests on uncertain forecasts, the discount protects you if growth disappoints, margins shrink or your model is simply wrong. It is usually expressed as a percentage of intrinsic value; many value investors look for 20 to 50 percent, and more for riskier or harder-to-predict businesses. The idea also explains why disciplined investors may sit on cash when nothing is cheap enough. A common confusion: in cost accounting the same phrase means how far actual or budgeted sales can fall before a firm reaches its break-even point. The investing meaning is about price versus value, not sales versus break-even.
example: Say you estimate the intrinsic value of ABC Ltd at ₹500 per share and buy only at ₹375. Your margin of safety is (500 - 375) / 500 = 25%, so your estimate could be ₹125 too high and you would still not have overpaid.
formula: Margin of safety = (Intrinsic value - Market price) / Intrinsic value x 100

short: Describes a share or asset whose market price is below what it is estimated to be truly worth.
kid: A shop sells a big box of crayons for the price of a small one. Getting more than you pay for feels like finding a bargain.
detail: An asset is undervalued when its market price sits below an estimate of its intrinsic value, whether that estimate comes from a DCF model, a comparison of multiples with peers, or the value of its assets. Shares can become undervalued when investors overreact to bad news, ignore small or unfashionable companies, or sell in a broad panic. Value investors hunt for such gaps, expecting the price to rise as the market recognises the true worth. In India, analysts often call a state-owned PSU stock undervalued when it trades at a low P/E or below book value compared with private peers. The common confusion is to equate a low P/E with undervaluation: a stock can be cheap because its business is genuinely deteriorating, a situation known as a value trap. Undervaluation is always a judgement that depends on the assumptions behind the estimate.
example: Say your DCF puts the value of XYZ Ltd at ₹1,200 per share while it trades at ₹900. It looks undervalued by ₹300, and the price would have to rise about 33% (300 / 900) to reach your estimate.

short: Describes a share or asset whose market price is above what it is estimated to be truly worth.
kid: Someone wants 10 coins for one small sweet that usually costs 2. If you pay that much, you get less than you paid for.
detail: An asset is overvalued when its market price sits above an estimate of its intrinsic value. Overvaluation often builds during periods of excitement, when investors extrapolate recent growth too far, chase momentum or crowd into a popular theme, as in the dot-com bubble of 1999-2000. Warning signs analysts watch include P/E or EV/EBITDA multiples far above the company's own history and its peers, and prices that imply growth the business is unlikely to deliver. In Indian market commentary, small-cap and IPO frenzies are often described as frothy or rich valuations. The common confusion is to assume an overvalued stock must fall soon: expensive stocks can stay expensive, or rise further, for a long time, and high-quality firms with long growth runways may justify high multiples. Overvaluation is a judgement about risk and expected return, not a timing signal.
example: Say your estimate of the intrinsic value of XYZ Ltd is ₹1,250 per share, but it trades at ₹2,000. On your numbers it is overvalued by ₹750, and the price would have to fall 37.5% (750 / 2,000) to reach your estimate.

short: A way to value a business by forecasting the cash it will generate and converting those future amounts into today's money.
kid: A coin you get next year is worth a little less than a coin in your hand today, because you have to wait. To value a lemonade stand, you add up all the coins it will make, counting later coins a bit less.
detail: Discounted cash flow valuation estimates an asset's intrinsic value as the present value of the cash it is expected to produce. Analysts usually forecast free cash flows for five to ten years, estimate a terminal value for all the years after that, and discount everything back at a rate that reflects risk: WACC for free cash flow to the firm, which gives enterprise value, or the cost of equity for free cash flow to equity, which gives equity value directly. DCF is the backbone of equity research, investment banking and project appraisal because it ties value to fundamentals rather than market mood. Its weakness is sensitivity: small changes in the discount rate or terminal growth rate can swing the answer widely, and the terminal value often makes up most of the total. Treat a DCF as a structured way to test assumptions, not a precise answer.
example: Say ABC Ltd is expected to generate free cash flow of ₹110 crore next year and ₹121 crore the year after, with a terminal value of ₹1,331 crore at the end of year 2. At a 10% discount rate, value = 110 / 1.10 + (121 + 1,331) / 1.21 = 100 + 1,200 = ₹1,300 crore.
formula: Value = sum of FCFt / (1 + r)^t for t = 1 to n + TVn / (1 + r)^n, where r is the discount rate and TVn is the terminal value at the end of year n

short: The cash a business has left from its operations after paying for the investment needed to maintain and grow it.
kid: Your lemonade stand brings in coins, but you must buy new lemons and fix the table. The coins left after that are yours to keep, share or save.
detail: Free cash flow is the cash a company generates after covering operating costs, taxes, working capital needs and capital expenditure. The simplest version is cash flow from operations minus capex. It matters because it is the cash actually available to repay debt, pay dividends, buy back shares or fund acquisitions, and it is harder to dress up than accounting profit. Valuation uses two precise versions: free cash flow to the firm, available to all capital providers, and free cash flow to equity, left for shareholders after debt payments. In India, investors watch FCF closely in sectors like infrastructure and telecom, where heavy capex can keep it negative even while reported profits rise. The common confusion is equating it with net profit or EBITDA: a profitable company can still burn cash, and negative FCF is not always bad if the spending earns more than its cost of capital.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports cash flow from operations of ₹500 crore and spends ₹320 crore on new machinery. Its free cash flow is ₹500 crore - ₹320 crore = ₹180 crore, which it could use for dividends, buybacks or debt repayment.
formula: FCF = Cash flow from operations - Capital expenditure

hl: free cash flow to the firm
short: Cash a business generates after taxes and reinvestment but before any payments to lenders, available to both lenders and shareholders.
kid: Your lemonade stand earns coins and buys new lemons. The coins left, before you give anything back to the friend who lent you some, belong to everyone who helped start the stand.
detail: Free cash flow to the firm is the cash generated by a company's operations after taxes, capital expenditure and working capital investment, but before interest and principal payments. Because it ignores how the company is financed, it is also called unlevered free cash flow. FCFF belongs to all capital providers, so in a DCF it is discounted at the weighted average cost of capital, and the result is enterprise value; subtracting net debt then gives equity value. This is the most common DCF set-up in investment banking and equity research because it values the business separately from its capital structure. A frequent mistake is mixing cash flows and discount rates: discounting FCFF at the cost of equity, or FCFE at WACC, gives a wrong answer. Interest is left out of FCFF because its tax benefit is already captured through the after-tax cost of debt in WACC.
example: Say ABC Ltd has EBIT of ₹200 crore, a 25% tax rate, depreciation of ₹40 crore, capex of ₹60 crore and an increase in working capital of ₹10 crore. FCFF = 200 x (1 - 0.25) + 40 - 60 - 10 = 150 + 40 - 60 - 10 = ₹120 crore.
formula: FCFF = EBIT x (1 - Tax rate) + Depreciation and amortisation - Capital expenditure - Increase in net working capital

short: Cash left for a company's shareholders after it pays its costs, taxes, reinvestment needs and what it owes lenders, plus any new borrowing.
kid: After your lemonade stand buys lemons and pays back the friend who lent you coins, the coins still left belong to you and your partners.
detail: Free cash flow to equity is the cash available to a company's shareholders after operating expenses, taxes, capital expenditure, working capital needs and all payments to lenders, adjusted for any new borrowing. Because it is measured after debt flows, it is also called levered free cash flow. FCFE shows how much a company could pay out as dividends or buybacks without raising new equity, so it is a better gauge of payout capacity than the dividends actually declared. In a DCF, FCFE is discounted at the cost of equity, which gives equity value directly without a bridge from enterprise value. It is commonly used for banks and other financial firms, where debt is part of operations and FCFF is hard to define. A common mistake is inflating FCFE by assuming endless new borrowing: net borrowing should match a stable, sustainable debt level.
example: Say ABC Ltd has net income of ₹80 crore, depreciation of ₹20 crore, capex of ₹45 crore, a working capital increase of ₹5 crore and net new borrowing of ₹10 crore. FCFE = 80 + 20 - 45 - 5 + 10 = ₹60 crore available to shareholders.
formula: FCFE = Net income + Depreciation and amortisation - Capital expenditure - Increase in net working capital + Net borrowing

short: The estimated value of all of a business's cash flows beyond the years an analyst forecasts in detail, expressed as one lump sum.
kid: You can guess how many apples your tree will give in the next few years, but not in every year after that. So you make one big guess for all those later years and add it on.
detail: Terminal value captures the value of a company's cash flows after the explicit forecast period of a DCF, usually five to ten years, on the assumption that the business keeps operating indefinitely. It is calculated in two main ways: the perpetuity growth, or Gordon growth, method, which assumes cash flows grow at a steady rate forever, and the exit multiple method, which applies a valuation multiple such as EV/EBITDA to the final year's figure. The terminal value is then discounted back to today along with the forecast cash flows. It matters because it often makes up 60 to 80 percent of total DCF value, so its assumptions dominate the result. The common mistake is forgetting to discount it: the formula gives a value as of the end of the forecast period, not today. Analysts often cross-check the two methods against each other.
example: Say a company's free cash flow in year 5 is ₹100 crore, expected to grow 5% a year forever, with a 10% discount rate. Terminal value at the end of year 5 = 100 x 1.05 / (0.10 - 0.05) = ₹2,100 crore, and its value today is 2,100 / 1.10^5, about ₹1,304 crore.
formula: Perpetuity growth: TV = FCFn x (1 + g) / (r - g); Exit multiple: TV = Final-year metric (such as EBITDA) x Exit multiple

short: The steady yearly rate at which a valuation assumes a company's cash flows will keep growing forever, once the detailed forecast years end.
kid: A tree grows fast when it is young, then only a tiny bit each year once it is big. This is that tiny, steady bit of growing that we expect to go on always.
detail: The terminal growth rate, g, is the constant annual growth rate assumed for free cash flows in every year after the explicit forecast period in a perpetuity-growth terminal value. Because the business is assumed to grow at this rate forever, g must be sustainable: it should not exceed the long-run nominal growth rate of the economy the company operates in, or the firm would eventually become larger than that economy. Many analysts use a rate close to long-run inflation plus real GDP growth, so rupee-based valuations usually use a higher g than dollar-based ones, reflecting India's higher expected inflation and growth. The rate must also be below the discount rate, otherwise the formula breaks down. The common mistake is picking a high g to justify a target price: because terminal value is so large, raising g by even one percentage point can lift the valuation sharply.
example: Say year-5 free cash flow is ₹100 crore and the discount rate is 11%. With g = 4%, terminal value = 100 x 1.04 / (0.11 - 0.04) = about ₹1,486 crore; with g = 5%, it is 100 x 1.05 / (0.11 - 0.05) = ₹1,750 crore, about 18% higher from a one-point change.
formula: TV = FCFn x (1 + g) / (r - g), where g is the terminal growth rate and must be less than the discount rate r

short: A stream of equal or steadily growing payments that continues forever, whose total value today can still be calculated.
kid: Imagine a magic tree that drops one apple for you every single day, forever. Even though the apples never stop, you can still say how much the tree is worth today.
detail: A perpetuity is a series of cash flows that continues indefinitely. For a level perpetuity paying C each period, the present value is C divided by the discount rate, because payments far in the future are worth almost nothing today. A growing perpetuity rises at a constant rate g each period, and its present value is the next payment divided by (r - g), which only works when r is greater than g. Examples include perpetual bonds such as the additional tier 1 bonds issued by Indian banks, irredeemable preference shares abroad, and the British consols that were redeemed in 2015. The formula is central to valuation because DCF terminal values and the Gordon growth model are growing perpetuities. Common errors are using this year's payment instead of next year's in the growing formula, and forgetting that the result is a value one period before the first payment.
example: A perpetuity paying ₹1,000 a year at a 10% discount rate is worth 1,000 / 0.10 = ₹10,000 today. If the ₹1,000 due next year then grows 4% a year forever, it is worth 1,000 / (0.10 - 0.04), about ₹16,667.
formula: PV of perpetuity = C / r; PV of growing perpetuity = C1 / (r - g), where C1 is next period's payment and r must exceed g

short: A formula that values a share as next year's dividend divided by the gap between investors' required return and a constant dividend growth rate.
kid: A hen lays eggs for you every year, and a few more each year. If you know how many eggs come next year and how fast that grows, one simple sum tells you what the hen is worth.
detail: The Gordon growth model, named after economist Myron Gordon, is the simplest dividend discount model. It assumes dividends grow at a constant rate g forever, so a share's value is next year's dividend divided by the required return on equity minus g. It works best for mature, stable companies with predictable payouts, such as utilities or established consumer goods firms, and the same growing-perpetuity formula is used for terminal value in a DCF. Rearranged, it also gives an estimate of the cost of equity: dividend yield plus growth. It fits poorly for fast-growing companies or those that pay no dividend. The model breaks down when g approaches or exceeds r, producing huge or negative values, and it is extremely sensitive to small changes in either input. A common mistake is plugging in the dividend just paid, D0, instead of next year's dividend, D1.
example: Say ABC Ltd will pay a dividend of ₹12 per share next year, dividends grow 6% a year, and shareholders require 12%. Value = 12 / (0.12 - 0.06) = ₹200 per share.
formula: P0 = D1 / (r - g), where D1 = D0 x (1 + g), r is the required return on equity and g is the constant dividend growth rate

short: Estimating a business's worth at the end of a forecast by multiplying its final-year earnings by the multiple at which similar companies trade.
kid: To guess what your lemonade stand will be worth in five years, you look at what people pay for stands like yours. If they pay 8 times what a stand makes in a year, you multiply your yearly coins by 8.
detail: The exit multiple method calculates a DCF's terminal value by assuming the business is sold at the end of the forecast period for a multiple of a financial metric, most often EV/EBITDA, sometimes EV/EBIT, EV/sales or P/E. The multiple is typically taken from current trading comparables or precedent transactions, and the resulting terminal value is discounted back to today. Investment bankers and private equity firms favour it because it mirrors how deals are priced and how funds plan exits. Its weakness is that it imports today's market mood into a supposedly intrinsic valuation: if peers trade at inflated multiples, the DCF inherits that. Analysts should check the multiple against the growth rate it implies under the perpetuity growth method. A common error is mismatching the metric: an EV multiple applied to EBITDA gives enterprise value, not equity value.
example: Say ABC Ltd's EBITDA in year 5 is ₹150 crore and comparable companies trade at 8x EV/EBITDA. Terminal value at the end of year 5 = 150 x 8 = ₹1,200 crore; at a 10% discount rate its present value is 1,200 / 1.10^5, about ₹745 crore.
formula: TV = Final-year EBITDA (or other metric) x Exit multiple

short: A valuation adjustment that treats each year's cash as arriving midway through the year, not all on the last day.
kid: A shop does not get all its coins on the last day of the year; they trickle in every day. So we pretend they all arrive in the middle of the year, which is closer to the truth.
detail: The mid-year convention assumes a company's free cash flows arrive evenly through each year, so they are discounted as if received at the midpoint: 0.5 years for year 1, 1.5 years for year 2, and so on, instead of at year-end. Because cash is treated as arriving six months earlier, valuations come out somewhat higher, by roughly half a year of discounting. It is standard in investment banking DCF models for businesses with steady, year-round cash flows, such as consumer or IT services companies. Two consistency points cause errors. A terminal value from the perpetuity growth method is usually discounted with the same mid-year timing, since it extends the same cash flow stream, while a terminal value from an exit multiple is discounted at the full year-end period, because it represents a sale price on that date. The convention suits lumpy or highly seasonal cash flows less well.
example: Say ABC Ltd expects ₹100 crore of free cash flow in year 1 and the discount rate is 10%. Year-end discounting gives 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.9 crore, while the mid-year convention gives 100 / 1.10^0.5 = ₹95.3 crore.

short: A way to value a share by adding up, in today's money, all the dividends, or cash payouts, it is expected to pay shareholders.
kid: A hen gives you eggs every week. To know what the hen is worth today, you count all the eggs she will ever give you, counting far-away eggs a little less.
detail: The dividend discount model values a share as the present value of all expected future dividends, discounted at the cost of equity. The logic is that dividends are the only cash a share ever delivers to an investor who holds it forever; even a future sale price simply reflects the dividends expected after that point. The simplest version is the Gordon growth model, which assumes constant growth, while multi-stage versions allow faster growth first and slower growth later. DDM suits mature, steady dividend payers such as utilities, large banks and established FMCG companies, including many dividend-paying public sector firms in India. It struggles with companies that pay little or no dividend, or that return cash mainly through buybacks, which is why analysts often prefer FCFE or FCFF models. A common mistake is assuming dividends equal earnings: payout ratios change, and dividends can be cut.
example: Say XYZ Ltd will pay dividends of ₹10 and ₹11 per share over the next two years, after which you expect to sell the share for ₹130, and you require 10%. Value = 10 / 1.10 + (11 + 130) / 1.21 = 9.09 + 116.53, about ₹125.62 per share.
formula: P0 = sum of Dt / (1 + r)^t for t = 1 to infinity, where Dt is the dividend in year t and r is the cost of equity

short: A dividend-based share valuation that allows faster dividend growth for some years before settling into slower, steady growth forever.
kid: A puppy grows very fast at first, then slows down and grows just a little once it is a big dog. This way of counting treats the fast years and the slow years differently.
detail: Multi-stage dividend discount models relax the Gordon model's single growth rate. In a two-stage DDM, dividends grow at a high rate for a set number of years, then at a stable rate forever; the share's value is the present value of the high-growth dividends plus the present value of a Gordon-model terminal price at the end of the first stage. A three-stage model adds a transition phase in which growth declines gradually, suiting companies that mature over a decade. The H-model, a shortcut developed by Fuller and Hsia, assumes growth falls in a straight line from a high rate to a stable rate over a period, where H is half that period. These models suit growing firms that already pay dividends, such as many Indian private banks and consumer companies. A common mistake is keeping one cost of equity across stages even when risk and payout are expected to change.
example: Say ABC Ltd just paid ₹10 per share, dividends grow 20% for two years and then 5% forever, and you require 12%. D1 = ₹12, D2 = ₹14.40, and the price at the end of year 2 = 14.40 x 1.05 / (0.12 - 0.05) = ₹216. Value = 12 / 1.12 + (14.40 + 216) / 1.12^2, about ₹194.39 per share.
formula: Two-stage: P0 = sum of Dt / (1 + r)^t for t = 1 to n + [D(n+1) / (r - gL)] / (1 + r)^n; H-model: P0 = D0 x (1 + gL) / (r - gL) + D0 x H x (gS - gL) / (r - gL), where gS is the initial high growth rate, gL the long-run rate and H half the length of the decline period

short: A way to value shares: the company's accounting net worth plus today's worth of future profits beyond what shareholders require on it.
kid: Your piggy bank already has 10 coins. If it can also earn extra coins beyond what you would normally expect, it is worth the 10 coins plus those extra ones.
detail: The residual income model values equity as current book value per share plus the present value of expected residual income. Residual income is net income minus a charge for the cost of equity on the opening book value, that is, profit above shareholders' required return. If a company earns exactly its cost of equity, residual income is zero and the share is worth its book value; consistently higher returns justify a price above book. The model, formalised by Edwards, Bell and Ohlson, is popular for banks, insurers and firms with negative or irregular free cash flow, and because much of the value is recognised early, it relies less on terminal value than a DCF does. A common confusion is with economic value added: EVA applies the same idea to all capital using NOPAT and WACC, while residual income focuses on equity.
example: Say XYZ Ltd has a book value of ₹100 per share, expects earnings of ₹15 per share next year and has a 12% cost of equity. Residual income = 15 - 0.12 x 100 = ₹3; if that ₹3 continues forever, value = 100 + 3 / 0.12 = ₹125 per share.
formula: V0 = B0 + sum of (Et - r x Bt-1) / (1 + r)^t, where B is book value per share, E is earnings per share and r is the cost of equity

short: A company's operating profit after subtracting a fair charge for all the money invested in it; positive means it is creating value.
kid: Your friend lends you 10 coins for a stand and wants 1 coin back as a thank-you. If the stand earns you 3 coins, you really made 2 extra coins after thanking your friend.
detail: Economic value added, a trademarked version of economic profit popularised by consultants Stern Stewart in the 1990s, measures the profit a business earns above the full cost of the capital it uses. It is calculated as net operating profit after tax minus a capital charge equal to WACC times invested capital, which equals invested capital times the spread between return on invested capital and WACC. A company can report healthy accounting profit yet have negative EVA, because accounting profit ignores the cost of equity. Companies use EVA to set targets, judge divisions and link executive pay to value creation. In valuation, a firm's value equals its invested capital plus the present value of future EVA. The common confusion is with residual income, which applies the same idea to equity alone, using net income and the cost of equity.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns NOPAT of ₹150 crore on invested capital of ₹1,000 crore, and its WACC is 12%. EVA = 150 - 0.12 x 1,000 = ₹30 crore, which matches (15% ROIC - 12% WACC) x ₹1,000 crore.
formula: EVA = NOPAT - (WACC x Invested capital) = (ROIC - WACC) x Invested capital

short: The part of a share's price that comes from expected future growth, beyond what the company would be worth if it never grew.
kid: A small apple tree gives 5 apples now. People pay extra for it because they believe it will grow big and give many more apples later. That extra is for the growing.
detail: PVGO splits a share's price into two parts: the value of the company if it simply kept its current earnings flat forever, and the extra value investors place on future growth from new investments. The no-growth value is earnings per share divided by the cost of equity, so PVGO is the share price minus EPS divided by r. PVGO is positive only when a firm can reinvest at returns above its cost of capital; growth funded by projects earning less than that cost destroys value, even if earnings rise. For high P/E stocks, such as many Indian consumer and new-age technology companies, PVGO is often more than half the price, meaning investors are paying mainly for growth that has yet to happen. The common confusion is equating PVGO with growth itself: it measures the value of profitable growth, and it can be negative.
example: Say XYZ Ltd trades at ₹500 per share, earns ₹25 per share and its cost of equity is 10%. The no-growth value is 25 / 0.10 = ₹250, so PVGO = 500 - 250 = ₹250, meaning half the price is a bet on future growth.
formula: PVGO = Share price - (EPS / Cost of equity)

short: Working backwards from a share's current price to find the growth and profits the market must be expecting to justify it.
kid: If a toy costs 50 coins, you can ask how much fun it must give to be worth that. You start from the price and work out the fun, instead of the other way round.
detail: A reverse DCF flips the usual valuation process. Instead of forecasting cash flows to estimate value, the analyst takes the current market price as given and solves for the assumptions, usually revenue or cash flow growth over a forecast period, that make the DCF equal that price. The investor then judges whether those implied expectations are realistic given the company's history, industry and competition. The approach, popularised by Alfred Rappaport and Michael Mauboussin in their book Expectations Investing, reduces the danger of building a model to confirm a view you already hold. It is widely used to debate premium-valued stocks, such as high P/E Indian consumer or platform companies, where the question is whether the price already bakes in a decade of rapid growth. A common mistake is treating the implied growth rate as a forecast: it is what the market requires, not what will happen.
example: Say a share trades at ₹1,000, next year's free cash flow to equity is ₹25 per share and the cost of equity is 11%. Solving 1,000 = 25 / (0.11 - g) gives g = 8.5%, so the price assumes cash flows grow 8.5% a year forever.
formula: Solve for the growth g that makes Market price = DCF value; single-stage version: Implied g = r - FCF1 / Price

short: The total value of a company's operating business, roughly what a buyer would pay for all its shares plus its debt, minus its cash.
kid: Buying a lemonade stand means paying the owner and also paying off what the stand owes. If there are coins in its till, you get those back, so you take them away from the price.
detail: Enterprise value measures the value of a company's core operations to all providers of capital, lenders as well as shareholders. The usual market-based calculation starts with equity market capitalisation, adds total debt, preference shares and minority interest, and subtracts cash and non-operating investments. Because EV does not depend on capital structure, it is the right numerator for ratios built on pre-interest measures such as EBITDA, EBIT or sales, which makes firms with different debt levels comparable. It is also the output of a DCF that discounts free cash flow to the firm at WACC. A common confusion is equating EV with market capitalisation or with the price paid for the shares: a debt-free company with lots of cash can have an EV well below its market cap, while a heavily indebted one has an EV far above it. In Indian headlines EV usually means electric vehicle, so read the context.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 crore shares at ₹200, a market capitalisation of ₹2,000 crore, debt of ₹800 crore and cash of ₹300 crore. EV = 2,000 + 800 - 300 = ₹2,500 crore. If its EBITDA is ₹250 crore, EV/EBITDA is 10x.
formula: EV = Market capitalisation + Total debt + Preference shares + Minority interest - Cash and cash equivalents

short: The value belonging only to a company's shareholders; for a listed company, its share price times the number of shares.
kid: If a lemonade stand is worth 10 coins but still owes 3 coins to a friend, only 7 coins really belong to the owner. That part truly belongs to the owner.
detail: Equity value is the portion of a company's total value that belongs to its ordinary shareholders after all prior claims, such as debt, preference shares and minority interests, are accounted for. For a listed company the market version is market capitalisation, ideally using fully diluted shares. In a valuation, equity value is either computed directly by discounting free cash flow to equity at the cost of equity, or derived from enterprise value by subtracting net debt and other non-equity claims. Dividing equity value by diluted shares gives value per share, the number compared with the market price. Equity value is the right numerator for multiples based on post-interest figures, such as P/E with net income or P/B with book value. The common confusion is mixing it up with enterprise value, for example quoting a deal's headline price without saying whether it includes the target's debt.
example: Say a DCF gives XYZ Ltd an enterprise value of ₹5,000 crore, and it has debt of ₹1,500 crore and cash of ₹500 crore. Equity value = 5,000 - 1,500 + 500 = ₹4,000 crore; with 20 crore diluted shares, that is ₹200 per share.
formula: Equity value = Enterprise value - Net debt - Preference shares - Minority interest + Non-operating assets; for a listed firm, Market equity value = Share price x Diluted shares outstanding

short: A company's total borrowings minus its cash and easily sold investments; a negative figure means it holds more cash than debt.
kid: You owe your sister 10 coins but have 4 coins in your piggy bank. If you paid her with those, you would still owe 6. That 6 is what you really owe.
detail: Net debt is gross borrowings, short-term and long-term, minus cash, cash equivalents and liquid investments that could be used to repay them. It gives a truer picture of leverage than gross debt, because a company sitting on cash is less risky than one with the same loans and no cash. Net debt is the main adjustment in the enterprise value bridge and the numerator of the widely watched net debt to EBITDA ratio. When cash exceeds debt, the company is said to have net cash or to be net debt free, a milestone Indian companies often highlight in investor presentations. Definitions vary: some analysts include lease liabilities, which have appeared on Indian balance sheets under Ind AS 116 since 2019, and pension deficits, while others exclude cash that is trapped or needed for daily operations. Always check what a company or broker report includes.
example: Say ABC Ltd has long-term loans of ₹600 crore, short-term borrowings of ₹150 crore, and cash and liquid investments of ₹250 crore. Net debt = 600 + 150 - 250 = ₹500 crore. If its cash were ₹900 crore instead, it would have net cash of ₹150 crore.
formula: Net debt = Short-term debt + Long-term debt - Cash and cash equivalents - Liquid investments

hl: enterprise value to equity value bridge
short: The step-by-step list of additions and subtractions that converts the value of a whole business into the part belonging to its shareholders.
kid: A house is worth a lot, but the family still owes some of it to others and has a jar of coins inside. Taking away what is owed and adding the coins shows what is truly theirs.
detail: The enterprise value bridge, or EV to equity bridge, reconciles the value of the operating business with the value of the ordinary equity. Starting from enterprise value, you subtract every claim that ranks ahead of or alongside shareholders, such as debt, lease liabilities, preference shares, minority (non-controlling) interests and unfunded pension obligations, and add non-operating assets that EV leaves out, such as cash, investments in associates and surplus land. Dividing the result by fully diluted shares gives value per share. It is a core step in DCFs and deal pricing, and the same items take you from market capitalisation to EV in reverse. Consistency is the main pitfall: any claim whose cash flows were excluded from free cash flow must appear in the bridge, and assets whose income is already in the cash flows must not be added again. Cross-holdings in Indian groups with listed subsidiaries often cause errors.
example: Say ABC Ltd has an enterprise value of ₹10,000 crore, debt of ₹2,500 crore, lease liabilities of ₹300 crore, minority interest of ₹200 crore, cash of ₹700 crore and a stake in an associate worth ₹300 crore. Equity value = 10,000 - 2,500 - 300 - 200 + 700 + 300 = ₹8,000 crore; with 40 crore diluted shares, that is ₹200 per share.
formula: Equity value = Enterprise value - Debt - Lease liabilities - Preference shares - Minority interest - Pension deficits + Cash + Non-operating assets

short: The total number of shares a company would have if all employee options and other rights to new shares were turned into shares.
kid: You cut a cake into 8 slices, but you promised 2 more friends a slice too. To be fair, you count 10 slices, so each slice is a bit smaller.
detail: Fully diluted shares count all existing shares plus the new shares that would be created if in-the-money stock options, warrants, restricted stock units and convertible bonds or preference shares were converted. Using this count matters because these instruments give their holders a claim on the company's value, so dividing equity value by basic shares alone overstates value per share. Options are usually added with the treasury stock method: it assumes holders exercise and the company uses the exercise money to buy back shares at the current price, so only the net new shares count. Convertibles are included when conversion is worthwhile, using the if-converted method. In India, ESOP pools at listed technology and new-age companies can be a meaningful source of dilution. A common mistake is using the basic share count, or including out-of-the-money options that holders would never exercise.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 100 crore shares trading at ₹50 and 10 crore employee options with an exercise price of ₹30. Exercise brings in 10 crore x ₹30 = ₹300 crore, which buys back 300 / 50 = 6 crore shares, so net new shares are 4 crore and fully diluted shares are 104 crore.
formula: Treasury stock method: Net new shares = Options x (1 - Exercise price / Share price); Fully diluted shares = Basic shares + Net new shares from options + Shares from convertibles

short: Valuing a company by comparing its price with similar businesses using ratios such as price to earnings, instead of forecasting its cash.
kid: To know a fair price for your bike, you look at what similar bikes sold for. If those went for about 20 coins, yours is probably worth about that too.
detail: Relative valuation estimates what an asset is worth by looking at how the market prices comparable assets, standardised by a common measure. Analysts pick a multiple, such as P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/sales, price-to-book or a sector-specific one like EV per tonne of capacity for cement, take the median or average for a peer group, and apply it to the company's own figure. The two main forms are comparable company analysis, using listed peers, and precedent transactions, using prices paid in past deals. It is quick, intuitive and reflects current market sentiment, which is why most broker reports and Indian IPO price bands are justified with peer multiples. Its weakness is that it only tells you whether something is cheap relative to others: if the whole sector is overvalued, so is your answer. Differences in growth, risk, margins and accounting must be adjusted for before comparing.
example: Say listed peers of ABC Ltd trade at a median P/E of 20x, and ABC expects earnings of ₹40 per share next year. A relative valuation gives 20 x ₹40 = ₹800 per share, before adjusting for any differences in growth or risk.
formula: Implied value = Peer multiple x Company's own metric (for example, Implied share price = Peer P/E x EPS)

short: Valuing a company by looking at the ratios, like price to earnings, at which similar listed companies currently trade on the stock market.
kid: To guess what your toy car might sell for, you look at the price tags on toy cars just like it in the shop today.
detail: Comparable company analysis, or trading comps, values a business using the current market multiples of similar listed companies. The analyst selects a peer group matched on industry, size, growth, margins and geography, gathers each peer's market data and financials, calculates multiples such as EV/EBITDA, EV/sales and P/E, and applies the median or a chosen range to the target's own figures. It is a standard part of investment banking pitch books, IPO pricing and equity research; in India, under SEBI rules as of 2025, an IPO document's basis for offer price section compares the issuer's ratios with listed peers. Comps reflect what investors are paying today, so they include market sentiment. Weaknesses: true peers can be scarce, especially for unusual businesses, and differences in accounting or year-ends distort comparisons. A common mistake is mixing equity-based and enterprise-based figures, or using trailing numbers for some peers and forward numbers for others.
example: Say three listed peers trade at EV/EBITDA multiples of 9x, 11x and 13x, giving a median of 11x. If ABC Ltd has EBITDA of ₹200 crore, its implied enterprise value is 11 x 200 = ₹2,200 crore, within a range of ₹1,800 crore to ₹2,600 crore.
formula: Implied enterprise value = Peer median EV/EBITDA x Target EBITDA; Implied equity value = Peer median P/E x Target net income

short: Valuing a company by looking at the prices buyers paid for similar whole companies in past takeovers and mergers.
kid: To decide what to ask for your whole lemonade stand, you find out what other kids got when they sold their whole stands.
detail: Precedent transaction analysis values a company using the multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar businesses. The analyst collects relevant deals, usually from the last few years in the same sector, computes each deal's enterprise value divided by the target's EBITDA, revenue or another metric at the time, and applies the range to the company being valued. Because buyers taking full ownership usually pay a control premium, often 20 to 40 percent over the pre-deal share price, precedent multiples typically come out higher than trading comps. This makes the method central to M&A advisory, fairness opinions and negotiating sale prices. Its weaknesses are that deal data can be incomplete, especially for private Indian transactions, and that each deal reflects the market conditions, synergies and competitive bidding of its own time. A common mistake is relying on stale deals from a very different market cycle without adjusting.
example: Say three recent acquisitions of similar companies were done at 10x, 12x and 14x EBITDA. If ABC Ltd has EBITDA of ₹150 crore, the median of 12x implies an enterprise value of 12 x 150 = ₹1,800 crore in a sale, compared with ₹1,500 crore if listed peers trade at 10x.
formula: Implied enterprise value = Median transaction EV/EBITDA x Target EBITDA
